subject: Physics
description: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, mechanical advantage

questions.stem: A seesaw is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Lever classes by position of fulcrum (F), load (L), effort (E): 1st class — F between L and E (seesaw, crowbar, scissors, pliers); 2nd class — L between F and E (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener); 3rd class — E between F and L (tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm, ice tongs). Mnemonic 'FLE-123' — F in middle for 1st, L middle for 2nd, E middle for 3rd.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The 'mechanical advantage' of a simple machine is defined as:

options.option_text: Input work divided by output work

questions.explanation: Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Load / Effort. If MA > 1, the machine multiplies force (lift a heavy load with a small effort, e.g., lever, pulley, jack). If MA < 1, the machine multiplies speed / distance (e.g., human arm as a 3rd-class lever — small movement at the joint → large movement at the hand). An ideal (frictionless) machine conserves work — input work = output work.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A single fixed pulley — such as the one on a flagpole — has a mechanical advantage of:
questions.explanation: A single fixed pulley simply changes the direction of the applied force — pulling down to lift something up — but does not reduce the effort (MA = 1). A movable pulley gives MA = 2 (halves the effort but doubles the distance pulled). Block-and-tackle systems (multiple-pulley sets) can reach MA of 4, 6 or higher.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: An inclined plane makes lifting a load easier by:

options.option_text: Spreading the work over a longer distance (less force, more distance)

questions.explanation: An inclined plane (ramp) doesn't reduce work done — it lets you use a smaller force over a longer distance. Work = Force × distance is the same. Effort force = (load × height) / ramp length. Shallower ramp → easier push, but longer way. Ramps have been used since ancient construction (Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, modern freight loading).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The six classical 'simple machines' include: lever, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw and:
questions.explanation: The six simple machines — lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, screw — were defined by Renaissance scientists; earlier Greek / Roman thinkers recognised five. A wedge is effectively a moving inclined plane (axe, knife). A screw is a wrapped inclined plane. Gears, springs, pistons are NOT simple machines — they are compound or later additions.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: A 200 N load is lifted with an effort of 50 N using a pulley system. The mechanical advantage is:
questions.explanation: MA = Load / Effort = 200 / 50 = 4. So a system of 4 pulleys (or an equivalent block-and-tackle) that halves the force twice over would do this. Trap answer 0.25 is Effort / Load (inverted formula). The student needs to lift the rope through 4× the distance the load rises — standard trade-off.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: An axe used to split wood is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: An axe — sharp edge narrowing to a point — is a wedge. It concentrates a large downward force into a small cross-section, splitting the wood fibres apart. Other wedges — knives, chisels, nails, pins. Wedges are effectively 'moving inclined planes'. The narrower (longer) the wedge, the greater the mechanical advantage — but the more strokes you need.
